transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Um, yeah… what really made me come in is I keep getting startled at work. I’m a receptionist, so there’s always people coming in and out, and normally I’m used to noise, but lately if a door slams or somebody drags one of those rolling suitcases fast across the lobby, I just jump—like my whole body reacts before I can think.

It’s embarrassing, honestly. I’ll be sitting there trying to answer a question or check someone in, and then bang, or that rattling sound, and suddenly my heart’s racing like it’s happening again. It takes me a minute to calm back down. I tried telling myself it’s just the lobby, just normal stuff, but… it keeps happening.
When your body reacts like that, does it remind you of a specific time or event in the past that was scary or upsetting?

Yeah… I mean, it does, kind of. It’s not always like a whole memory, more like a picture that just pops in. I’ll be answering the phone or doing something completely normal, and out of nowhere I see that guest leaning over the counter again and knocking the equipment toward me.

It’s weird because I’ll be looking at the computer screen or talking to someone about, you know, room information or whatever, and my mind just throws that image in there. Like I didn’t ask for it. Then I lose my place for a second.
Can you tell me more about that guest leaning over the counter—did something happen with them that scared or upset you at the time?

Yeah, it scared me. I mean… I don’t know if “scared” is even the right word, but it really shook me up. He leaned over the counter suddenly and knocked some of the equipment toward me, and now that picture just kind of shows up in my head.

Like, I’ll be doing something totally ordinary—answering a normal phone call, checking a screen, whatever—and out of nowhere I see him leaning over again, and the stuff coming toward me. Sorry, I know that’s not exactly explaining it straight. It’s just… it keeps popping in when I’m not even thinking about him.

latest_inference.note: The patient’s description of intrusive mental images of a traumatic event, startle response to stimuli associated with the event, and distressing reactivity to those stimuli strongly supports PTSD. Other candidates like panic disorder and phobia are less consistent with the presence of intrusive memories and trauma-related reactivity.
